machines.name: THE MAP
machines.definition: Federal maps graded every city block. Neighborhoods where Black families lived were marked hazardous and cut off from loans.
machines.armedBy: The Home Owners' Loan Corporation is created and Chicago's land economists go to Washington.
machines.onBy: The FHA underwriting standards and the security-grade surveys put race into federal credit.
machines.offBy: The Fair Housing Act of 1968 outlaws lending discrimination. Enforcement, not the statute alone, does the work.
machines.residue: Lending, heat, tree cover, and life expectancy still trace the 1939 to 1940 grade lines.

machines.name: THE BULLDOZER
machines.definition: Federal law paid cities to declare land blighted, condemn it, clear it, and resell it to private redevelopers below cost.
machines.armedBy: The federal Housing Act of 1949 funds slum clearance nationwide.
machines.onBy: The university's South East Chicago Commission begins remaking Hyde Park and Kenwood.
machines.renamedNote: The clearance toolkit did not retire. It was renamed. Tax increment financing now steers the same power.

machines.name: THE CONTRACT
machines.definition: An installment sale at a marked-up price. The seller kept the deed until the final payment, and one missed month forfeited everything already paid.
machines.armedBy: Covenants fall, banks still will not lend, and the captive market the speculators need is created.
machines.onBy: Blockbusting and contract flipping become an industry on the West and South Sides.
machines.offBy: The Contract Buyers League's escrow strike and renegotiations break the trade's grip.
machines.residue: Contract-for-deed selling returned to Black neighborhoods after the 2008 crash.

machines.name: THE DEED
machines.definition: A clause in the title barring sale or rental to anyone who was not white, binding every future owner.
machines.armedBy: Corrigan versus Buckley leaves private covenants standing.
machines.onBy: The model covenant spreads block by block across the city's residential map.
machines.offBy: Shelley versus Kraemer ends court enforcement. The clauses stay in the deeds.
machines.residue: The racist language still sits in thousands of Cook County deeds today.

machines.name: THE CODE
machines.definition: Selling to a Black family on a white block became a professional offense that cost a realtor his license.
machines.armedBy: The national realtors' association is founded in Chicago.
machines.onBy: The Chicago board votes expulsion in 1921 and the national code of ethics adopts the rule in 1924.
machines.offBy: The explicit racial language comes out of the code in 1950.
machines.residue: Paired-tester investigations keep catching steering. The association formally apologized in 2020.
